h1: Body Idioms: Say It Without Saying It
sub: English is full of idioms that use body parts — but the words don't mean what they say! Read the clues, compare them to Spanish, and crack the locks.
kw: idioms body hand arm leg heart english spanish lend a hand echar una mano costar un ojo figurative language multilingual ESL grade 4

brief.label: Your mission
brief.h: Figure out what the idioms really mean
brief.p: An idiom is a phrase whose meaning you cannot get by adding up the words. Notice the trap (the literal picture), find the real meaning, and compare English to Spanish. Your home language is a clue, not a problem!

win.p: You told the literal picture apart from the real meaning and compared two languages. That is exactly how strong readers handle figurative language.

clues.title: To 'lend a hand'
clues.body: To 'lend a hand' means to help someone. You do not really give away your hand! In Spanish, people say 'echar una mano' (throw a hand) — the same picture: a hand.

clues.title: To 'cost an arm and a leg'
clues.body: If something 'costs an arm and a leg,' it is very expensive. Spanish uses a different body part: 'costar un ojo de la cara' (to cost an eye of the face) — an eye, not an arm and a leg.

clues.title: To 'pull someone's leg'
clues.body: To 'pull someone's leg' means to joke or tease them, not to touch their leg. Spanish says 'tomar el pelo' (to take the hair) — a different picture, but the same idea: kidding around.

clues.title: How idioms work
clues.body: In every idiom, the words do not add up to the meaning. Good readers use the sentence around it (context) to find the real meaning — and compare it to how their own language says the same thing.

clues.title: Same idea, different picture
clues.body: Languages often share an idea but paint it with different pictures. Sometimes the picture matches (hand = mano); sometimes it changes (arm and a leg → an eye). Noticing this makes you a language detective.

clues.title: True, but off-topic
clues.body: The adult human body has 206 bones. That is a true science fact about the body — but it has nothing to do with what these idioms mean.

locks.title: What does it really mean?
locks.q: What does 'cost an arm and a leg' really mean?
options: You must give someone your arm and your leg
It hurts your arm and your leg
locks.reason: Clue 2 says it means 'very expensive.' The literal picture — giving away body parts — is the trap. Idioms almost never mean what the words literally say.

locks.title: What is true about idioms?
locks.q: Check every statement that is TRUE about idioms (use the clues). Leave out the one that is false.

items.t: An idiom's meaning is not the sum of its words
English 'lend a hand' and Spanish 'echar una mano' use the same picture — a hand
Different languages can share an idea but paint it with a different picture
You can always understand an idiom by translating each word by itself

locks.reason: The false statement is the trap: translating word-by-word is exactly what does NOT work for idioms. The three true statements come straight from the clues.

locks.title: Put the joke in order
locks.q: Tap the three lines of the conversation in the ORDER that makes 'pull my leg' make sense.
locks.reason: The joke only works in order: the surprising claim, then the question 'Are you pulling my leg?' (Are you kidding me?), then the reveal that it was a joke. Idioms depend on context.

locks.title: Compare the two languages
locks.q: In English we 'lend a hand.' In Spanish, people say 'echar una ___' — the SAME body part. Type that body part in English OR Spanish.
locks.reason: Both languages use the hand: English 'hand,' Spanish 'mano.' Your home language is a clue — when the picture matches across languages, it helps you remember the idiom.

h1: Animal Idioms: When Words Go Wild
sub: English idioms are full of animals — but nobody is really talking about pets! Read the clues, compare them to Spanish, and crack the locks.
kw: idioms animals cat dog bird horse english spanish raining cats and dogs llueve a cántaros a little bird told me pajarito hold your horses figurative language multilingual esl grade 4 5

brief.label: Your mission
brief.h: Find the real meaning behind the animals
brief.p: An idiom is a phrase whose meaning is not the sum of its words. These use animals — but the meaning is hidden. Find it, and compare English to Spanish. Your home language is a clue!

win.p: You looked past the animals to the real meaning and compared two languages. That is exactly how strong readers handle figurative language.

clues.title: 'Raining cats and dogs'
clues.body: 'It's raining cats and dogs' means it is raining very hard — not that animals are falling! Spanish uses a different picture: 'llueve a cántaros' (it's raining pitchers).

clues.title: 'Hold your horses'
clues.body: 'Hold your horses' means wait, be patient — even if there are no horses. Spanish says 'para el carro' (stop the cart) — a different picture, same idea: slow down.

clues.title: 'A little bird told me'
clues.body: 'A little bird told me' means someone told me a secret and I won't say who. Spanish says 'me lo dijo un pajarito' (a little bird told me) — the SAME picture: a little bird!

clues.title: 'Let the cat out of the bag'
clues.body: 'Let the cat out of the bag' means to reveal a secret by accident. There is no real cat. Spanish says 'descubrir el pastel' (uncover the cake) — a very different picture, same idea.

clues.title: How the picture travels
clues.body: Across languages, an idea can keep the same picture (little bird = pajarito) or change it (cats and dogs → pitchers). Spotting which is which makes you a language detective.

clues.title: True, but off-topic
clues.body: An elephant is the largest land animal and can weigh over 6 tons. That is a true animal fact — but it has nothing to do with what these idioms mean.

locks.title: What does it really mean?
locks.q: What does 'it's raining cats and dogs' really mean?
options: Animals are falling from the sky
You should bring your pets inside
locks.reason: Clue 1 says it means raining very hard. The literal picture — falling animals — is the trap. Idioms almost never mean what the words say.

locks.title: What is true about idioms?
locks.q: Check every statement that is TRUE (use the clues). Leave out the false one.

items.t: An idiom's meaning is not the sum of its words
English 'a little bird told me' and Spanish 'me lo dijo un pajarito' use the SAME picture — a little bird
'Hold your horses' means to wait and be patient
You can always tell what an animal idiom means by thinking about the animal

locks.reason: The false statement is the trap: the animal is a picture, not the meaning. The three true statements come straight from the clues.

locks.title: Put the talk in order
locks.q: Tap the three lines in the ORDER that makes 'hold your horses' make sense.
locks.reason: The order shows the meaning: one person rushes, the other says 'hold your horses' (wait), and then they agree to wait. Idioms depend on context.

locks.title: Compare the two languages
locks.q: In English a secret came from 'a little ___.' In Spanish, 'me lo dijo un ___' (pajarito). Type that animal in English OR Spanish.
locks.reason: Both languages use the bird: English 'bird,' Spanish 'pájaro/pajarito.' When the picture matches across languages, it helps you remember the idiom.

h1: Food Idioms: It's Not About Lunch
sub: English is packed with food idioms — but none of them are really about eating! Read the clues, compare them to Spanish, and crack the locks.
kw: idioms food cake bread beans apple bacon english spanish piece of cake pan comido spill the beans bring home the bacon figurative language multilingual esl grade 4 5

brief.label: Your mission
brief.h: Find the meaning hidden in the food
brief.p: An idiom's meaning is not the sum of its words. These use food — but the real meaning is hidden. Find it, and compare English to Spanish. Your home language is a clue!

win.p: You looked past the food to the real meaning and compared two languages — exactly how strong readers handle figurative language.

clues.title: 'A piece of cake'
clues.body: 'A piece of cake' means something very easy — not a dessert! Spanish says 'pan comido' (eaten bread) — a different food, same idea: easy.

clues.title: 'Spill the beans'
clues.body: 'Spill the beans' means to reveal a secret. No beans are spilled! Spanish says 'descubrir el pastel' (uncover the cake) — a different picture, same idea.

clues.title: 'The apple of my eye'
clues.body: 'The apple of my eye' means someone you love and treasure. Spanish says 'la niña de mis ojos' (the girl of my eyes) — a different picture, but it keeps the eye.

clues.title: 'Bring home the bacon'
clues.body: 'Bring home the bacon' means to earn money for the family. Spanish says 'ganarse el pan' (earn the bread) — a different food, same idea: earning a living.

clues.title: Same idea, different food
clues.body: Across languages, the idea stays but the 'food' changes: cake → bread, bacon → bread. Noticing the swap makes you a language detective.

clues.title: True, but off-topic
clues.body: The world's largest pizza was over 13,000 square feet. That is a true food fact — but it has nothing to do with what these idioms mean.

locks.title: What does it really mean?
locks.q: What does 'a piece of cake' really mean?
locks.reason: Clue 1 says it means very easy. The literal picture — a slice of cake — is the trap. Idioms almost never mean what the words say.

locks.title: What is true about idioms?
locks.q: Check every statement that is TRUE (use the clues). Leave out the false one.

items.t: An idiom's meaning is not the sum of its words
English 'bring home the bacon' and Spanish 'ganarse el pan' both mean to earn a living
'A piece of cake' means something very easy
Every food idiom is really about cooking or eating

locks.reason: The false statement is the trap: the food is a picture, not the meaning. The three true statements come straight from the clues.

locks.title: Put the talk in order
locks.q: Tap the three lines in the ORDER that makes 'a piece of cake' make sense.

pads.e: 😎 'Don't worry — it's a piece of cake.'

locks.reason: The order shows the meaning: worry, reassurance ('a piece of cake'), then success. Context is what unlocks an idiom.

locks.title: Compare the two languages
locks.q: Both idioms name a food that means 'easy': English 'a piece of cake,' Spanish 'pan comido.' Type the English food OR the Spanish food.
locks.reason: English uses 'cake,' Spanish uses 'pan' (bread) — a different food, the same meaning: easy. Comparing the two builds language awareness.
